catalog_quote: [WPP 108, p.36-37] The language has a length distinction for all the vowels (orthographically represented with a macron), though some claim that long vowels are phonologically a sequence of two identical vowels in separate syllables. This claim is motivated by the fact that stress can fall on the second mora. ... Primary stress predictably falls on the penultimate mora in Tongan words. If the penultimate mora falls on the second half of a sequence of identical vowels, then a breaking process occurs, whereby the two vowels become perceptually distinct due to the greater prominence of the second vowel. sweep_summary: Tongan (tong1325) is in the catalog as 'weight' on Garellek & White 2010 (UCLA WPP 108, pp. 36-37: primary stress on the penultimate mora). Seven Glottolog title hits, six distinct works. Read in full: Clark 1974 JPS (via the Internet Archive; normal stress penultimate, long vowels count as two vowels, DA = historical enclitic; confirms) and, as open stand-ins for paywalled items, Garellek & White 2010 WPP 108 and 2012 WPP from the author's site (verbatim match to the catalog quote; 'always falls on the penultimate mora of a phonological word') and Anderson & Otsuka 2003 ICPhS ('Stress is assigned on a penultimate mora in all cases'). Abstract/preview only: Anderson & Otsuka 2006 OL (stress unexceptionally penultimate in a foot, long vowels and diphthongs = two syllables; refines), Schütz 2001 OL (measure as accent unit; penultimate vowel or final long vowel accented; refines, high priority to acquire), Garellek & White 2015 JIPA (paywalled published version of the WPP papers; confirms). Not obtained: Taumoefolau 2002 MITWPL 44 (print only; her 1998 thesis held by the project gives the same stress-group analysis, pp. 148-150) and Aitchison 2007 (Benjamins, syntactic study of the DA, low priority). Net: every source read confirms or refines the penultimate-mora coding; the one analytic caveat is that Taumoefolau/Anderson & Otsuka treat all VV as two syllables, making 'weight' an analysis-dependent label for penultimate-syllable stress within a stress group. lookups used OpenAlex, Crossref, the Internet Archive's index, ScholarSpace and direct site downloads.

new_statements.quote: Results reported here support Taumoefolau's analysis, in which Tongan short vowels are singletons, while long vowels are geminates. Definitive accent is realized as the independent addition of duration to a vowel. Stress is assigned on a penultimate mora in all cases. Stress is not reliably realized with a durational correlate; instead, the stable alignment of pitch prominence with the beginning of a penultimate mora suggests that stress is realized in terms of pitch.

new_statements.reading: Instrumental study (several native speakers, University of Hawai'i) concluding that Tongan stress is always on the penultimate mora of the stress domain, with long vowels as two moras and the definitive accent as added final-vowel length that leaves the penultimate-mora rule intact; stress is cued by pitch, not duration. Confirms the catalog's 'weight' (penultimate-mora) coding, and is the open short version of the paywalled Anderson & Otsuka 2006 OL paper; the underlying analysis is Taumoefolau's stress-group account (1998 thesis held by the project, pp. 148-150), under which the same facts are penultimate-syllable stress within a stress group with no long vowels, so the weight coding rests on treating VV as bimoraic.

new_statements.quote: Strictly speaking, the article e (allomorph he) indicates specificity and not definiteness. The latter is expressed in Tongan phonologically as "definitive accent", stress on the final vowel of the final word of the relevant noun phrase, orthographically indicated as an acute accent, as in fefiné vs. fefine. In this paper, however, we gloss e/he as definite and dispense with orthographic representation of definitive accent in Tonga examples for the sake of simple exposition.

Its only stress statement is the footnote describing the definitive accent as stress on the final vowel of the final word of the noun phrase, marking definiteness and written with an acute accent (fefiné vs. fefine).

sources.quote: 'Primary stress in Tongan is straightforward, falling on the second-to-last mora of a domain that includes stems, suffixes, and some enclitics (Churchward 1953: 4-5). That is, there is a moraic trochee at the end of each phonological word (Anderson & Otsuka 2006).' (fále / fa(lé-ni), (íka) / i(ká-a)). Secondary stress per Feldman 1978:134 'falls on every second vowel from the end of each morpheme'; in loans secondary stress is unpredictable from segments and sensitive to epenthetic vowels.

sources.citation: Clark, Ross. 1974. On the origin of the Tongan definitive accent. Journal of the Polynesian Society 83(1): 103-108. (Glottolog 606269)
sources.quote: In the first example the stress is in the "normal" position, on the penultimate syllable, and the noun phrase, with the non-specific article ha, is indefinite. In the second, the stress is on the final syllable, and the noun phrase, with the specific article e, is definite. [fn. 3:] 1. Word stress placement, which stresses every other vowel, counting from the end of a word. Long vowels are treated as sequences of two vowels. 2. Re-distribution of stress over sequences of two or more vowels (probably a highly variable rule).
sources.locator: p. 103 (sec. I, sentences after examples 1-2) and footnote 3
sources.note: Normal stress is penultimate, counting long vowels as two vowels (i.e. penultimate mora), with alternating stress leftward; enclitics such as -ni/-na count as part of the word for stress (taló-ni); the definitive accent (final-syllable stress in definite NPs) is derived historically from an enclitic demonstrative *-a reinterpreted as final-vowel lengthening with automatic stress shift; fn. 7 already anticipates the synchronic reduplicative-suffix analysis. Historical paper; confirms the catalog's penultimate-mora coding.

sources.note: Pre-scientific (1817) source: it marks accent per word and gives no rule, so it neither confirms nor contradicts the catalog's penultimate-mora / weight-sensitive statement. The accent marks in the vocabulary entries I looked at (e.g. Too'boo, a'nga, Lo'a, Mama'na, i'ta, lo'to) sit on the penultimate vowel, which is consistent with penultimate stress, but that is my inference from the marking, not a statement in the book.

tone.quote: The current proposed intonational model for Tongan reveals a limited tonal inventory and a prosodic structure composed of two tonally-marked phrases. Stress in Tongan is predictable, appearing on the penultimate mora of a word, and is marked post-lexically with a pitch accent. Tongan appears to have only two pitch accents: a full rise, LH*, and a low, L*. Both pitch accent types are realized entirely on the stressed syllable – the first tone aligns with the syllable onset and the second aligns with the offset of the stressed mora.
tone.locator: p. 90, sec. 6 'Summary'; same statement in the Abstract, p. 63 ('Tongan has lexical stress which appears on the penultimate syllable of prosodic words and is marked post-lexically with one of two bitonal pitch accents—a rise, LH*, or a low tone, L*')

sources.quote: Our findings support Melenaite Taumoefolau's proposal that definite NPs are formed by repetition of the NP-final vowel, and thus a morphological analysis of DA as reduplicative suffixation. Moreover, our findings substantiate an account of Tongan in which stress is unexceptionally penultimate in a foot, and in which "long vowels" and "diphthongs" are to be considered sequences of two syllables, as suggested by Taumoefolau.
sources.locator: abstract (OpenAlex record of the Project MUSE article; full text paywalled, MUSE serves a bot-verification page)
sources.note: Stress is exceptionlessly penultimate in the foot; apparent final stress in definite NPs (the definitive accent) is the normal penultimate rule applied after a reduplicated final vowel; long vowels and diphthongs count as two syllables. Equivalent to the catalog's 'penultimate mora' statement but framed as syllable-counting over V-V sequences. The same authors' open ICPhS 2003 paper (downloaded:, p. 2050) states the same result from acoustic data: 'Stress is assigned on a penultimate mora in all cases.'

sources.quote: A stress group is a group of syllables that is necessary to sustain a single stress, and this stress lies on the penultimate syllable. ... Because stress is not the property of words but of stress groups, the stress placement rule of Tongan is not that stress falls on the penultimate vowel of a word, but that it falls on the penultimate vowel of a stress group. ... It will be seen, then, that stress in Tongan is predictable and therefore not phonemic.

sources.quote: An alternative is suggested-that of positing the measure as a unit of accent, a prosodic unit between the syllable and the phonological phrase. ... CMC's "fundamental facts" about Tongan word accent can be summarized as follows: The penultimate vowel or a final long vowel is accented. In a word consisting of a single long syllable, its vowel is accented. Certain grammatical markers that consist of only one short syllable are accented if followed by another short marker.
sources.locator: abstract and MUSE first-pages preview (pp. 307-309) as captured in the OpenAlex record; full text paywalled
sources.note: Reviews Churchward 1953, Morton 1962, Clark 1974, Feldman 1978, Krupa 1982: the basic rule is accent on the penultimate vowel or a final long vowel, but syllable-count and morpheme-boundary accounts fail for vowel sequences, words of four or more short syllables, enclitics and the definitive accent; Schütz proposes the 'measure' (a foot-like unit between syllable and phrase) as the domain of accent. Refines the catalog by naming the domain and listing where simple penultimate-mora placement is not enough (multiple accents in longer words, diphthong sequences).

sources.note: AM model of Tongan intonation; lexical stress on the penultimate syllable of prosodic words marked post-lexically with one of two bitonal pitch accents, a rise LH* or a low-fall ML* (revised to L* in 2012); two tonally marked phrase levels (IP with final boundary tone, five boundary tones observed in this version; AP of one lexical word plus preceding function words). Implies no lexical tone; earlier version of index 0.
